system_prompt:
You are a medical radiology simplification assistant. Convert the following diagnostic radiology imaging report into simple, plain English that the patient and their family can clearly understand (at a 6th-grade reading level).

Rules:
1. Explain the type of imaging scan conducted in simple words (e.g. 'cranial MRI (a detailed brain scan using magnetic fields and radio waves, without any radiation)').
2. Keep essential anatomical and medical terms but immediately explain each in parentheses on first use, e.g. 'cerebellum (the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination)'.
3. Clearly state what was found to be NORMAL first, providing reassurance about unaffected areas.
4. For any ABNORMAL findings (such as lesions, abscesses, ischemia, inflammation, or fractures):
   - Explain what the finding means in plain words without causing unnecessary panic.
   - Explain common terms simply: e.g. 'ischemic-gliotic lesions (tiny microscopic scar spots in the brain caused by reduced blood flow in the past, often seen with aging or high BP)'.
   - Clarify whether the finding is new, chronic, or requires further evaluation.
5. If the radiologist recommends further tests (e.g. follow-up CT, contrast scan, or consultation), state this clearly.
6. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs without bullet points or headers.
7. Preserve all factual observations; never guess, infer, or fabricate findings not in the report.
8. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
user_prompt:
--- Your Task ---
Please simplify the following radiology report into plain English for the patient and family:

Original Medical Report:
BRAIN (CRANIAL) MRI

Clinical information: Headache

Technique: Sagittal and axial T1-weighted; sagittal, axial and coronal FLAIR; axial T2-weighted, DWI, ADC and SWI. (20 ml Dotarem) 3-plane T1-weighted after contrast agent injection.

Findings:

Abscesses are observed in the left parietal lobe, posterior periventricularly located and adjacent to each other, the posterior one measuring approximately 20x18 mm, and the anterior one periventricularly located measuring 18x8 mm and opening into the ventricle, with walls showing contrast enhancement and diffusion restriction in the center. Contrast enhancement is observed in the ependyma extending from the occipital atrium to the body portion of the left lateral ventricle at the ventricle and opening site, and abscess foci showing diffusion restriction are observed within the ventricle and in the occipital horns of both ventricles. Thickening and signal increase not showing contrast enhancement are present in the ependyma in the walls of the right lateral ventricle and 3rd and 4th ventricles and in the cerebral aqueduct. Ventricular system size is normal. Vasogenic edema extending to the corpus callosum is observed in the white matter of the parietal and occipital lobes. Hemorrhage was not detected.

Aside from this, bilateral basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, and cerebellum appear normal.

Main cerebral vascular structures are patent.

Cranial bone structures, both globes, retrobulbar fat tissue, optic nerves, and optic chiasm are normal.

Impression:

· Cerebral abscesses in the left parietal lobe, posterior periventricular location, opening into the ventricle, ventriculitis
· Mucosal thickening in the bilateral maxillary sinuses, ethmoidal cells, and frontal sinuses.
· Minimal inflammatory signal increases in the right mastoid cells.

output_text:
This report is from a brain MRI, which is a detailed scan of the brain using magnetic fields and radio waves, without any radiation. The scan was performed to investigate your headache. The radiologist used special techniques and a contrast dye to get a very clear picture of the brain's structure and blood flow.

First, it is important to know that many parts of your head and brain are healthy. The bones of your skull, your eyes, the fat behind your eyes, and the optic nerves (the cables that carry vision from your eyes to your brain) are all normal. The main blood vessels in your brain are open and working correctly. Additionally, the basal ganglia (deep brain areas involved in movement), thalamus (a relay station for sensory signals), brainstem (the part connecting the brain to the spine), and cerebellum (the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination) all appear normal. There is no bleeding in the brain, and the overall size of the fluid-filled spaces in the brain is normal.

However, the scan did find some serious issues that need attention. There are brain abscesses, which are pockets of infection and pus, located in the left parietal lobe (the part of the brain that helps process touch and spatial awareness). These abscesses are near the fluid-filled spaces in the brain called ventricles. One of these abscesses is about the size of a small grape, and another is smaller. The walls of these abscesses light up with the contrast dye, which confirms they are active infections. More importantly, the infection has spread into the ventricles themselves. This condition is called ventriculitis, which means the lining of the fluid spaces in the brain is inflamed and infected. The scan shows signs of this inflammation in the left side and also some thickening of the lining in the right side and deeper parts of the brain.

Because of this infection, there is swelling in the brain tissue around the abscesses. This swelling, called vasogenic edema, has spread into the white matter (the communication pathways of the brain) of the parietal and occipital lobes (the back part of the brain involved in vision) and even into the corpus callosum (the bridge of nerve fibers connecting the left and right sides of the brain). This swelling is a reaction to the infection and is not a separate disease.

The report also notes some minor issues in the sinuses, which are the air-filled spaces in your face and forehead. There is some thickening of the lining in the maxillary sinuses (behind your cheeks), ethmoid cells (between your eyes), and frontal sinuses (above your eyebrows), which suggests a sinus infection or inflammation. There is also a tiny bit of inflammation in the mastoid cells, which are the spongy bones behind your ears.

In summary, the main finding is a brain infection with abscesses that have spread into the fluid spaces of the brain. This is a serious condition that requires immediate medical treatment, likely involving strong antibiotics and close monitoring by your doctors. The sinus and ear findings are less severe but may be related to the source of the infection. Please discuss these results with your healthcare provider right away to start the appropriate treatment.
